title: GitHub Actions from zero

story: You open a pull request in fcp, and before you can switch tabs a yellow dot appears under it: Unit Tests, in progress. Nobody pressed a button. You would like the PR to also show how many tests ran, so you add a small second job to the workflow file. It is called summary, and it reads coverage/summary.json, the file that the unit-tests job writes.

You push again. Unit Tests turns green, and summary turns red with one line: cat: coverage/summary.json: No such file or directory. The log of the first job clearly shows the file being written a few seconds earlier, in the same run of the same workflow.
hook.question: What does GitHub do between a push and a green check, and why can one job not see a file that another job just wrote?

read.h: From a push to a check
p: Five things are involved, so let us name them before we follow the flow. An event is something that happens in the repo, such as a push, a pull request being opened, or a timer going off. A workflow is one YAML file in the .github/workflows folder that says which events it cares about and what to do. A job is a list of steps that run together on one machine, and that machine is called a runner. A step is one shell command or one packaged action.

When an event happens, GitHub reads every workflow file in the commit, and each file whose on: block matches the event starts a run of that workflow. So one push can start several workflows at the same time; in the lab you will see one push to the actions/checkout repo start four of them. Inside each run, the jobs start on runners, the steps of each job run in order, and every job reports its result back to the commit, which is what you see as a check on the PR.

Here is the top of the workflow that made the yellow dot, shortened. Read it from the top: the name, the events, the permissions, then the jobs. The check on the PR is called Unit Tests because the job's name: says so on line 21.

code.text:
name: "[FRONTEND] - CI"
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    types: [opened, reopened, synchronize]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write

jobs:
  check-changes:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/_check-changes-reusable.yml
    with:
      component: frontend

  unit-tests:
    name: Unit Tests
    runs-on: fcp-runner-set
    needs: check-changes
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version: 24.15.0
      - run: npm ci
        working-directory: frontend

notes.text: on: lists the events that start this workflow: a push to main, a PR against main, or a click on Run workflow.
types narrows the pull_request event. Without it the workflow would also run when someone adds a label or an assignee.
workflow_dispatch adds a Run workflow button in the Actions tab. It needs no value after the colon.
What this workflow's token may do. The last section of this page explains it.
A job can call a whole other workflow file instead of listing steps. The next lesson is about this.
The job's name is the check's name on the PR. Rules that require a check refer to this exact text.
runs-on chooses the machine by a label. fcp-runner-set is our own pool of runners.
needs makes this job wait until check-changes has finished. Without needs, jobs start at the same time.
A uses step runs a published action. The long hash names one exact version; the next lesson explains why.

p: Inside a job, the steps run one after another, on the same machine and in the same folder. A run step is shell commands, exactly as if you typed them in a terminal. A uses step runs an action, a packaged step that someone published under the name owner/repo@version: actions/checkout clones your repo, and actions/setup-node installs Node. The runner starts with an empty folder, which is why almost every job begins with checkout. If a step fails, the steps after it are skipped and the job turns red.

Because the steps share a disk, a file that step 2 writes is still there for step 3. For a small value that later parts of the workflow need, a step writes name=value into a special file whose path GitHub puts in the variable $GITHUB_OUTPUT. The step also needs an id, so that others can refer to the value as steps.<id>.outputs.<name>. The ${{ }} around such a reference is an expression: GitHub replaces it with the value before the shell ever sees the line. That replacement is convenient, and it is also the reason for a whole lesson about safety later in this part.
Here is the workflow from the story. Read it once and try to spot both problems before the next section explains them.

code.text:
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  unit-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Count the tests
        id: count
        run: |
          mkdir -p coverage
          echo '{"tests": 412}' > coverage/summary.json
          echo "tests=412" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  summary:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: unit-tests
    steps:
      - run: cat coverage/summary.json
      - run: echo "Ran ${{ steps.count.outputs.tests }} tests"

notes.text: The id lets other steps of this job read this step's outputs.
Writing tests=412 into the $GITHUB_OUTPUT file publishes a value called tests.
This is the line that failed: the file was written on a different machine.
This would print 'Ran  tests' with nothing in the middle: steps.count only exists inside the unit-tests job.

read.h: Every job gets a fresh machine
p: Now the red summary job makes sense. Each job asks for a runner with runs-on, and it always gets a fresh one. A GitHub-hosted runner such as ubuntu-latest is a new virtual machine that GitHub throws away when the job ends. Our own label, fcp-runner-set, starts a new single-use container in our internal Kubernetes cluster for every job, and removes it afterwards. The unit-tests job wrote coverage/summary.json on its machine, and the summary job ran on another machine that never had the file. The line needs: unit-tests only made summary wait; it does not move anything.

Jobs without needs run at the same time, which is why a workflow with five jobs is not five times slower. When one job has to hand something to another, there are two ways. A small string goes through job outputs: the first job lists it under outputs, and the second job reads it as needs.<job>.outputs.<name>. A file goes through an artifact, which is a file that GitHub stores with the run: actions/upload-artifact saves it in the first job, and actions/download-artifact fetches it in the second. Here is the summary fixed with outputs. A linter called actionlint, which you will run in the lab, catches the steps.count mistake before you push; the missing file it cannot catch, because that only fails while the job runs.

code.text:
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  unit-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      tests: ${{ steps.count.outputs.tests }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Count the tests
        id: count
        run: echo "tests=412" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  summary:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: unit-tests
    steps:
      - run: echo "Ran ${{ needs.unit-tests.outputs.tests }} tests"

notes.text: The token may only read the repo. The next section explains why every workflow should say this.
The job publishes the step's value under its own name, so other jobs can read it.
needs.<job>.outputs is how a later job reads it. The needs: on line 23 is required for this to work.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why fresh machines are a feature
p: A fresh machine per job feels wasteful at first, because every job has to check out the code and install packages again. Caches such as the cache option of actions/setup-node make the install fast, but they never share a whole machine. The benefit is that nothing can stay behind: not a half-built folder from yesterday's run, and not a file planted by a stranger's pull request. Every job starts from the same clean state, so a green check means the same thing every time.
Our agent platform uses the same idea for the agents themselves: every agent run gets a brand-new virtual machine, and the machine is destroyed when the run ends.

read.h: What the job's token may do
p: Every job receives a token called GITHUB_TOKEN. GitHub creates it when the job starts, it works only on this one repository, and it expires when the job finishes, or after 24 hours at the latest. Actions such as checkout use it automatically, so you rarely see it. What it may do is set by the permissions block: each scope, such as contents or pull-requests, gets read, write or none. As soon as you write a permissions block, every scope you did not list becomes none. If you write no block at all, the job gets the default of the repository or the organization, and in older repositories that default is write access to almost everything.

So write the block in every workflow, with the smallest set that works. contents: read is enough to clone the code. pull-requests: write is needed to comment on a PR. id-token: write lets the job ask GitHub for an identity token that proves to a service such as AWS which repository and workflow it is; a later lesson in this part explains it. When a job needs more than its block allows, it does not fail quietly: the API call answers 403 Forbidden, and the log says which call it was.

deeper.h: Go deeper: three surprises worth knowing
p: First, a push or a comment that a workflow makes with GITHUB_TOKEN does not start new workflow runs, apart from workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch events. GitHub does this so that a workflow cannot trigger itself in an endless loop. A bot whose pushes should run CI, like our agents, uses a GitHub App token instead; a later lesson in this part covers Apps.

Second, workflows started by schedule (a cron timer, always in UTC) or by workflow_run (another workflow finished) always use the copy of the file on the default branch. You cannot try them from a branch: you merge the file first, then test it.

Third, a job that an if: condition skips reports its result as skipped, and a required check treats skipped as passing. That is useful when a job should not run for some changes, but it also means a skipped job proves nothing.

lab.title: Read a real run, then write your own
needs: The gh CLI, logged in (gh auth status); every gh call here only reads public repos
uv, so that uvx can run actionlint without installing it
lab.goal: Follow one real push from the event to its jobs and steps, then write a two-job workflow that passes a value between jobs and passes actionlint.

guess.q: The unit-tests job writes coverage/summary.json. The summary job says needs: unit-tests and runs cat coverage/summary.json. What happens?

options.text: It works, because needs makes summary wait until the file exists.
options.why: needs only decides the order. summary still runs on a different, fresh machine, where the file was never written.

options.text: summary fails with No such file or directory, because it runs on another machine.
options.why: Every job gets its own fresh runner. To hand over a file you need an artifact; to hand over a short value, job outputs.

options.text: It works, because GitHub copies the working folder to every job that needs it.
options.why: GitHub copies nothing between jobs by itself. Only outputs and artifacts cross from one job to another.

lab.build: Fix ci.yml so that summary prints the number of tests. Give the unit-tests job an outputs block that publishes tests from the count step, make summary read it with needs.unit-tests.outputs.tests, delete the cat line (the file stays on the first machine), and add a permissions block that only allows reading the repo. Run uvx --from actionlint-py actionlint .github/workflows/ci.yml again until it prints nothing.

The unit-tests job has an outputs: block whose value comes from steps.count.outputs.tests.
The workflow has a permissions: block with contents: read and nothing else.

name: CI

lab.fix: A teammate copied broken.yml from another repo and pushed it. GitHub showed only 'Invalid workflow file', and nothing ran for a week before anyone noticed. Run uvx --from actionlint-py actionlint .github/workflows/broken.yml. It finds four problems: a misspelled key under push, an invalid permission value, a job name in needs that does not exist, and a runner label it does not know. Fix the first three in the file. The fourth is not a mistake: fcp-runner-set is our own label, so tell actionlint about it in .github/actionlint.yaml (self-hosted-runner: labels: [fcp-runner-set]), the way fcp does.
explain: Why did needs: unit-tests not make the file appear in the summary job?
When would you pass something between jobs with outputs, and when with an artifact?
Why should every workflow have a permissions block, even one that only reads?
lab.done: actionlint is silent on both files, and you can say for each line of ci.yml which machine it runs on.

check.q: A workflow has two jobs, lint and test, and neither has needs. In what order do they run?

options.text: At the same time, each on its own fresh runner
options.why: Jobs only wait for each other when needs says so. Without it, GitHub starts them in parallel.

options.text: In the order they are written in the file: lint, then test
options.why: That is how steps inside one job behave. Jobs are independent unless needs connects them.

options.text: One after the other on the same runner, to save machines
options.why: Jobs never share a runner. Each job always gets a fresh machine of its own.

check.q: A workflow says permissions: contents: read. A step in it tries to post a comment on the pull request. What happens?

options.text: It works, because GITHUB_TOKEN can always comment on its own repo
options.why: Once a permissions block exists, every scope it does not list is none, including pull-requests.

options.text: It works, but only for the PR author's own comments
options.why: The token does not act as the PR author. What it may do is decided only by the permissions block.

options.text: The API call answers 403, because the block gave pull-requests no access
options.why: Listing one scope turns every other scope off. Commenting needs pull-requests: write.

check.q: You push one commit, and four different workflows start at once. Why?

options.text: GitHub runs every workflow in the repo on every push
options.why: A workflow only runs when its on: block matches the event. Files that only listen to, say, schedule do not start.

options.text: Four workflow files have an on: block that matches this push
options.why: GitHub checks every workflow file against the event, and each one that matches starts its own run.

options.text: The push was split into four events, one per changed folder
options.why: A push is one event. The number of runs comes from how many files listen for it.

p: Every check on an fcp pull request, including the ones on Nova's PRs, is a job like the ones in this lesson, and most of them run on fcp-runner-set, our own runners inside the internal cluster. Those runners can reach internal services that a GitHub-hosted machine cannot, which is why our platform's own small workflows use them too.

Three tickets build directly on this lesson. Before main can require the unit-test checks, the three jobs called Unit Tests get distinct names, and the on: path filters are removed, because a required check whose workflow never starts waits forever. The trigger service, our small internal service that turns a red CI run into one fixer run, is woken by a workflow_run workflow on fcp-runner-set. And every repo with workflows gets the same actionlint job you ran in the lab.

tickets.why: Renames the three 'Unit Tests' jobs and removes the paths: filters so the checks can be required on main.
The routine trigger: a workflow_run workflow on fcp-runner-set with a job-level if: on the branch name.
Adds actionlint (and zizmor) to every repo with workflows, with each repo's runner labels in .github/actionlint.yaml.

words.plain: Something that happens in a repo, such as a push, a pull request or a timer, that can start workflows.
One YAML file in .github/workflows that says which events start it and which jobs to run.
A list of steps that run in order on one fresh machine. Jobs run in parallel unless needs orders them.
The machine a job runs on, chosen by the runs-on label. It is new for every job.
A packaged, published step used as owner/repo@version, such as actions/checkout.
The short-lived token each job gets for its own repo. The permissions block decides what it may do.

review.q: Without looking, write a workflow with two jobs where the second prints a value that the first one computed.
review.a: The first job's step has an id and writes name=value to $GITHUB_OUTPUT; the job has outputs: name: ${{ steps.<id>.outputs.name }}; the second job has needs: <first> and reads ${{ needs.<first>.outputs.name }}.

review.q: A teammate's summary job cannot find a file the build job wrote. Explain the cause and both fixes.
review.a: Each job runs on its own fresh runner, so files do not cross. Upload the file as an artifact in the first job and download it in the second, or, if only a short value is needed, pass it through job outputs.

review.q: What does the permissions block do, and what happens to the scopes you leave out?
review.a: It sets what GITHUB_TOKEN may do, scope by scope (read, write or none). Once the block exists, every scope you did not list is none.

remember: An event starts every workflow that listens for it, each job runs on its own fresh machine, and the job's token can do only what permissions allows.
